title: 7. Why the Price Is What It Is: Valuation, Reverse DCF & Peer Comps

epigraph.quote: For the investor, a too-high purchase price for the stock of an excellent company can undo the effects of a subsequent decade of favorable business developments.
epigraph.author: Benjamin Graham, The Intelligent Investor

web_blocks.title: 7.1 Deconstructing Today's Price: The Scarcity Premium in Numbers

web_blocks.html: At the November 20, 2026 close of $1,102.15 per share, Costco carries a $488.40 billion market cap [26, 27]. Pre-dividend enterprise value stands at $477.28 billion [26, 27]. On November 10, 2026, the board declared a $30.00 per share special cash dividend (~$13.3 billion payable December 4, 2026) [19, 26]. Adjusting that cash out of net cash puts pro-forma enterprise value near $490.6 billion [19, 26]. On FY2026 audited earnings of $20.76 per diluted share and $9,390 million of free cash flow, the stock looks steep [6, 26, 27]. Shares trade at 53.09x trailing P/E, 43.85x forward P/E, 33.24x EV/EBITDA, and 52.06x Price-to-FCF (a 1.92% trailing FCF yield) [6, 26, 27].

Why does a physical retailer with an 11.09% gross margin and 3.85% operating margin trade at software multiples [6, 27]? The market is pricing in three traits at once. First, earnings are steady: $5,907 million in fees form an annuity floor equal to 50.6% of operating income [6, 18]. Second, negative working capital and 21.23% ROIC let Costco self-fund 30+ annual store openings while returning $13.3 billion in cash [6, 19, 27]. Third, defensive funds have crowded into the stock during uncertain macro regimes [27, 28, 29]. That crowding pushed trailing P/E 48% above its 10-year mean of 35.86x and Price-to-Book (13.65x) 45% above its 9.40x mean [27, 28, 29].

web_blocks.takeaway: Every major multiple sits 35% to 55% above Costco's 10-year average [27, 28, 29]. That premium leaves zero margin of safety if multiples compress [27, 28, 29].

web_blocks.title: 7.2 Reverse DCF: What Growth Rate Is Already Baked Into $1,102.15?

web_blocks.html: Instead of guessing a single target, a Reverse DCF solves for the growth baked into today's $488.40 billion market cap [26, 27]. We use an 8.5% cost of equity and a 3.5% terminal growth rate [26, 27]. Starting from FY2026 FCF of $9,390 million, we also note FY2027 capex rises to ~$7.5 billion from $6.44 billion [6, 16, 30]. To earn an 8.5% annual return, Costco must grow FCF at 14.0% to 14.5% per year for ten straight years [6, 16, 30]. That requires ~$35 billion in annual FCF by FY2036 [6, 16, 30].

Now compare that hurdle against Costco's audited 10-year track record from Pass 1 [6, 7]. From FY2017 to FY2026, revenue grew at 9.96% per year and operating income at 12.31% [6, 7]. Net income grew 14.72% per year, helped by 2017 U.S. tax cuts and higher interest income on cash [6, 7]. Consensus 5-year forward EPS growth sits at just 9.81% [27]. Suppose sales grow 7.5%–8.5% over the next decade and operating margin edges from 3.85% to 4.10%. Then FCF compounds closer to 9%–10%, pointing to fair value near $850–$950 per share [30]. That aligns with independent DCF models near $850.95 [30]. At $1,102.15, buyers pay upfront for flawless execution and permanent peak multiples.

web_blocks.title: Reverse DCF & Multiple-Normalization Intrinsic Value Check
web_blocks.how_calculated: We blend 2-year forward EPS ($25.40 FY28E EPS at 10.6% CAGR) with a 39.0x exit P/E, still ~9% above the 35.86x 10-year mean. We cross-check that against an 8.5% WACC DCF ($851–$950 range).
web_blocks.the_inputs: FY26 EPS $20.76; FY26 FCF $9,390M; 443.27M shares; 10-year avg P/E 35.86x; consensus 5Y EPS growth 9.81%.
web_blocks.if_off: If Costco sustains >13% EPS growth from faster global openings and retail media profit while rates fall, a 45x–48x multiple could hold.

web_blocks.title: 7.3 Quantitative Peer Comparison: Warehouse Clubs & Big-Box Rivals

web_blocks.caption: Costco vs. Listed Retail & Warehouse Club Peers (Live Session Snapshot: Nov 20, 2026)
web_blocks.takeaway: Costco posts the group's top ROIC at 21.23%, yet its 53.09x P/E and 4.47x PEG look steep [26, 27]. It trades far above BJ's (20.34x P/E), Target (15.39x), Amazon (19.95x), and Walmart (48.96x) [26, 27].

web_blocks.mechanism: By late 1999, Walmart was the world's top physical retailer, growing stores and profits steadily. Yet the market priced its shares at ~45x–50x earnings.
web_blocks.outcome_numbers: From FY2000 to FY2010, Walmart grew sales from $165B to $408B (+9.5% CAGR) and EPS from $1.25 to $3.72 (+11.5% CAGR). Still, the stock went sideways for over 11 years as its P/E fell from ~48x to ~14x.
web_blocks.lesson_for_symbol: Great business growth cannot save buyers from flat multi-year returns when entry multiples top 45x–50x on single-digit sales growth.

web_blocks.title: 7.4 Reverse DCF Sensitivity Matrix & Why 1.92% FCF Yield Leaves Zero Margin of Safety

web_blocks.html: Single-point DCFs can hide fragile inputs, so we stress-test $1,102.15 across a full sensitivity grid [26, 27, 30]. We vary WACC from 8.0% to 9.0%, terminal growth from 3.0% to 4.0%, and exit P/E from 34x to 42x [26, 27, 30]. The math stays unforgiving across every realistic cell. Even with a low 8.0% cost of equity and an aggressive 4.0% terminal growth rate, $488.40 billion still demands ~12.2% annual FCF growth for a decade [16, 27]. That sits well above the 9.81% consensus 5-year EPS growth rate and rising ~$7.5 billion FY2027 capex [16, 27]. At a standard 8.5% WACC and 3.5% terminal growth, a realistic 9.5% FCF CAGR yields $875–$915 per share [30].

Cash yield tells the exact same story. At $1,102.15, Costco's 1.92% trailing FCF yield (52.06x P/FCF) trails risk-free 5.04% 10-year U.S. Treasuries by 312 basis points [26, 27]. That negative spread leaves buyers reliant on long-term growth and high exit multiples. Suppose trailing P/E drops 20% from 53.09x to 42.5x over two years—still 19% above its 35.86x 10-year mean [27, 28]. Even then, shareholders lose nearly two full years of 10%+ earnings growth just to break even [27, 28].

web_blocks.caption: Reverse DCF Sensitivity: Implied 10-Year FCF CAGR Required to Justify $1,102.15 (Base FCF: $9,390M)
web_blocks.takeaway: Even at 8.0% WACC and 4.0% terminal growth, $1,102.15 bakes in ~12.2%–14.2% 10-year FCF growth. At a realistic 9.5% FCF pace, fair value sits near $850–$950 [30].

web_blocks.html: Valuation Re-Underwriting Trigger: A price reset to $850–$900 (~33x–35x forward EPS) or sustained >13% EPS growth from global openings and retail media would change our valuation verdict.

book_paragraphs: Now that you and I have completed our price-blind audit and locked in our verdict that Costco is an unmistakable COMPOUNDER_PASS business, we are finally allowed to lift the curtain on the stock ticker. What we see on the screen as of the November 20, 2026 close is a collision between one of the finest retail machines ever built and one of the most demanding price tags in public equity markets: $1,102.15 per share, representing a $488.40 billion market capitalization.

Let us put that $488.40 billion valuation into plain English. In FY2026, Costco generated $9,390 million of free cash flow. Dividing $9.39 billion by $488.40 billion gives you a trailing free cash flow yield of 1.92%. That means if you bought the entire company at today's market price and pocketed every dollar of cash left over after building new warehouses, your starting cash yield would be less than two cents on the dollar—well below risk-free U.S. Treasury yields. On earnings, you are paying 53.09 times trailing net income and 43.85 times forward earnings.

Why is the market willing to pay 53 times earnings for a business that caps its branded markups at 14% and earns a 3.85% operating margin? Because institutional capital prizes certainty above almost everything else. When investors look at Costco, they see $5,907 million in membership fees that recur at a 92.3% U.S. and Canada renewal rate, a negative working-capital cycle that funds expansion out of supplier payables, and a management team that just declared a $30.00 per share special cash dividend—roughly $13.3 billion handed back to owners. In a choppy macro tape, Costco has become a 'safety bond with growth'—and the crowd has bid its P/E nearly 50% above its own 10-year average of 35.86x.

To test whether $1,102.15 makes sense for your marginal dollar, you and I should run a Reverse DCF—not to predict the future, but to see what the market is already assuming. At an 8.5% discount rate and a 3.5% terminal growth rate, $488.40 billion requires Costco to grow free cash flow at roughly 14.0% to 14.5% every single year for the next decade. Think about how hard that is on a $303 billion revenue base. Over the past ten years—including the once-in-a-generation pandemic surge—Costco grew revenue at 9.96% annually, and consensus expects roughly 9.8% EPS growth over the next five years. And remember, management just guided FY2027 capital expenditures up to $7.5 billion from $6.44 billion.

History offers a sobering mirror here. At the peak of 1999, Walmart was the undisputed king of global retail. Over the next eleven years, Walmart more than doubled its sales from $165 billion to $408 billion and tripled its earnings per share. Yet shareholders who bought at 48 times earnings in 1999 endured a 'lost decade' of flat stock performance because the multiple compressed back toward earth. That is the exact valuation tension we face with Costco at $1,102.15: the business can execute brilliantly and the stock can still deliver mediocre returns if the P/E normalizes from 53x toward 36x–39x.

Let us push that Reverse DCF one step deeper together, because single-point valuation models can lull you into false precision. When you and I test a stock priced at $1,102.15, we want to see a full sensitivity grid: what happens if the discount rate moves between 8.0% and 9.0%, and what happens if perpetual terminal growth sits between 3.0% and 4.0%? Even if we hand Costco the most generous assumptions on the sheet—an 8.0% cost of equity and a 4.0% perpetual growth rate forever—$488.40 billion still demands roughly 12.2% annual free cash flow growth for ten straight years. At our baseline 8.5% WACC and 3.5% terminal growth, it demands 14.2% FCF growth every year through FY2036.

Now ask yourself whether 14.2% annual FCF compounding on a $303 billion revenue base is a conservative base case. Remember that management just guided FY2027 capital expenditures up to $7.5 billion from $6.44 billion in FY2026 to sustain 30-plus annual warehouse openings. When capex grows faster than revenue for a couple of years, free cash flow growth naturally lags operating income growth. If Costco compounds free cash flow at a very respectable 9.5% per year—right in line with its 9.96% ten-year revenue CAGR and 9.81% consensus five-year EPS growth—our 8.5% WACC model puts intrinsic value around $875 to $915 per share, right alongside independent DCF benchmarks near $851.

That brings us back to the simplest sanity check in finance: the 1.92% trailing free cash flow yield. When risk-free U.S. Treasuries pay more than 4%, accepting a 1.92% starting cash yield on an equity means you have zero margin of safety against multiple compression. Think about the arithmetic: if Costco's earnings grow 10.6% a year for two years—from $20.76 to $25.40—but its P/E eases just one-fifth of the way down from 53.09x to 42.5x, the stock goes nowhere. And if it normalizes to 39.0x—still higher than its 35.86x ten-year average—you get our $990.00 base-case value, a 10.2% capital loss from $1,102.15.

book_callouts.title: NARRATOR'S REFLECTION: GREAT COMPANY VS. GREAT STOCK
book_callouts.text: The hardest discipline in institutional investing is separating admiration for a business from the price of its shares. Costco earns 21.23% ROIC and treats its members with unmatched fairness—but at 53.09x trailing earnings and a 4.47x PEG ratio, the market has already collected several years of future compounding upfront.

book_subsections.title: Peer Multiples: Paying Twice BJ's Multiple for Half the Risk?
paragraphs: When you line Costco up against its direct listed peers on the November 20, 2026 tape, the valuation gap jumps off the page. BJ's Wholesale Club—a smaller regional U.S. warehouse club operator—trades at 20.34x trailing earnings and 12.09x EV/EBITDA. Target trades at 15.39x trailing earnings, and Amazon trades at 19.95x trailing earnings with a 0.87x PEG ratio. Even Walmart, which has enjoyed its own massive re-rating on grocery share gains and high-margin advertising, sits at 48.96x trailing P/E and 39.58x forward P/E—still cheaper than Costco on every multiple despite a 12.79% ROIC versus Costco's 21.23%.

Costco undeniably deserves a structural premium over BJ's and Target because its 21.23% ROIC, 94.9% owned-building footprint, and global scale in 14 countries are in a different league. The analytical question is not whether Costco deserves a premium; it is whether a 35% to 55% premium over Costco's own 10-year historical averages leaves enough upside to clear our 15% annualized return hurdle. Our Reverse DCF and 39x normalized FY2028E multiple point to $990 per share as fair value—below today's $1,102.15 quote.

book_subsections.title: Duration Risk: Why 53x Earnings Behaves Like a Long-Duration Bond
paragraphs: When you and I evaluate a 53.09x trailing P/E and a 1.92% free cash flow yield, it helps to borrow a concept from fixed income: duration. A stock trading at 15x earnings returns your purchase price in roughly fifteen years of flat earnings; a stock trading at 52x free cash flow pushes the majority of your economic payback decades into the future. That means your near-term return is extraordinarily sensitive to the exit multiple Mr. Market is willing to pay two or three years from now.

Think about how little has to go wrong for a 53x multiple to compress. Costco does not need to suffer a recession or lose its moat. All it takes is for Treasury yields to stay firm, or for comparable-store sales to cool from 6% to 4% while FY2027 capex steps up to $7.5 billion. If the market decides that a mature $303 billion retailer growing earnings at ~10% deserves 39x forward earnings—still a 9% premium above Costco's own 10-year historical average of 35.86x—then $25.40 of FY2028E EPS values the business at $990.00. At $1,102.15 today, you are paying $112.15 per share above that normalized destination. That is why Benjamin Graham warned that paying too high a price for an excellent company can neutralize a decade of operational brilliance.
